sentences.text: Sonselasuchus stood with a bipedal posture, featuring large eye sockets, toothless jaws, and an enlarged pubic boot.
Researchers suggest its snout may have supported a keratinous beak, a structure similar to those found in turtles and birds.
The genus name honors the Sonsela Buttes located on the Navajo Nation in Arizona.
Fossils were found in the Chinle Formation of Arizona, all originating from the Kaye Quarry discovered by Tom Kaye in 2014.
Over 950 disarticulated bones belonging to at least 36 individuals were collected from this site.
Elliott Armour Smith and Christian A. Sidor formally described this new genus and species in 2026.
Evidence suggests the animal was quadrupedal as an immature individual but shifted to bipedalism as it grew older.
It is classified as a member of the superfamily Poposauroidea and the family Shuvosauridae.
Phylogenetic analysis places Sonselasuchus in the Shuvosauridae clade in an unresolved relationship with Effigia and Shuvosaurus.
Sonselasuchus lived during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
